articles.title: No Atlantic Hurricanes (Yet)…
articles.summary: Looking at the satellite picture, there are no hurricanes in the Atlantic at this point, from Miami to the west coast of Africa, where the beginning stages o...
articles.body:
Looking at the satellite picture, there are no hurricanes in the Atlantic at this point, from Miami to the west coast of Africa, where the beginning stages of tropical systems can start to form. This includes the Caribbean and Gulf (not pictured), which are considered part of the "Atlantic Basin".

On the second graphic, you can see the average frequency of storms in the Atlantic basin, which had its peak last Thursday, September 10. Now we're past the peak and have not had one hurricane at all yet this season, which runs from June 1-Nov 30.

Records show that this is the first time this has happened in at least 60 years. We say 60 years on the 3rd graphic there because 1966 is the beginning of what's known as the satellite era. This was a huge tool in the meteorology arsenal because it gave us, for the first time, the ability to look at the entire oceans and waterways where hurricanes develop.

Now, as far as what is in the record books, you can go back to 1941 to find the last year when we didn't have a hurricane in the Atlantic Basin as of September 12th. But without satellite data, one can't be entirely sure that is accurate. Hurricanes could have formed undetected by ships, airplanes, and in between pieces of land in or close to the oceans, seas, gulfs, etc.

The strong El Niño is probably the biggest factor suppressing development in the Atlantic this year. But there are other factors such as Saharan Dust, which tends to dry out the atmosphere, and wind shear (wind changing speed and direction, especially with height), which tends to rip apart tropical systems.

But keep in mind, although this is great news for Atlantic and other coastal areas, the season is just past peak, and hurricanes could develop later this month and October because there is still plenty of warm water around (which tropical systems thrive on). For now, enjoy the ride, especially if you're vacationing in a hurricane-prone area.

Thanks to the meteorologists and folks at Accu-Weather for some of the background information in this article.

articles.title: Residents of Charholi battle lack of access roads, water & power woes
articles.summary: PUNE: For more than 10,000 residents living across eight housing societies in Charholi’s Pride World City township, stepping out of their neighbourhoo.
articles.body: PUNE: For more than 10,000 residents living across eight housing societies in Charholi’s Pride World City township, stepping out of their neighbourhood each day feels less like a commute and more like an ordeal.Nestled amid rapidly developing localities like Lohegaon, Dhanori, Wagholi and Kharadi, Charholi was marketed as Pune’s next residential hotspot.But behind the towering apartment complexes and promises of worldclass connectivity lies a very different reality: A township effectively dependent on a single lifeline road to Pune city limits, plagued by chronic traffic snarls, water shortages and erratic power supply. Residents say they are living in a neighbourhood that has grown faster than the infrastructure meant to support it.“We have just one access road to get to PMC limits, which for us is crucial as most of us work in companies in Kharadi, Magarpatta and Viman nagar. Access to the airport is also via this single road,” IT profession al Dhananjay Ashok Deshmukh said.“It passes through a narrow private road provided by Ajeen kya DY Patil University and then merges onto the already choked Porwal Road. If that private road is closed even for a day, more than 10,000 people would be as good as isolated. Other roads exist only on paper. On the ground, they are dead ends,” he said.Charholi's rapid growth was fuelled by ambitious promises of connectivity through the proposed outer and inner ring roads, and a 90mwide arterial road that was supposed to link to Wagholi and Spine Road.Years later, plans re main confined to blueprints while residents continue to navigate pot holed roads and gridlocked traffic. During school hours, the situation descends into complete chaos.“In mornings and after noons, when school buses enter the stretch, traffic comes to a standstill. If a PMPML bus and a school bus arrive from opposite directions, the road locks up entirely. Parents are anxious about letting children travel alone. On top of that, poor roads have led to multiple accidents, with bikers frequently skidding on damaged stretches,” resident Kshitija Tilekar said.Despite repeated attempts to engage with Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation (PCMC), resi dents claim they have largely been met with silence.“We don’t want another temporary fix,” IT professional Vinay Tatti said. “There are several roads that can be opened and integrated into a proper traffic plan. Some smaller internal roads could even function as oneway corridors to ease congestion. A parallel road to Porwal Road was acquired nearly three months ago, but no work has started. It remains inaccessible,” he said.For many, the consequences go far beyond inconvenience. Pune airport, located barely 7km away should be reachable within 1520 minutes. Instead, residents often spend more than an hour on narrow and congested approach roads.“Even ambulances struggle to reach us because of the traffic,” said resident Virendra Gambhir, who has lived here since 2018. Gambhir recalls experiencing this firsthand after suffering a serious fall in Dec 2020.“A hospital just 5km away took me nearly three hours to reach,” he said, add ing, “I was fortunate that someone offered me a ride because getting an auto or cab is almost impossible here. Even after being discharged, every followup visit became exhausting and stressful because of traffic and terrible roads.”According to Gambhir, complaints filed through PCMC’s Sarathi app and emails sent to officials between Dec 2020 and April 2022 yielded little result.“My online complaints were routinely closed without any resolution, and my emails went unan swered,” he said. Water Tank Next Door, But No Flow in Taps Roads are only one part of the crisis.Residents point to an over head water tank standing right beside the township as a symbol of the area’s infrastructure paradox. Despite its presence, households remain heavily dependent on tanker water supplied by the developer at subsidised rates. “We spend nearly Rs1 crore every year on tanker water,” said resident Dhruv Malhotra.“There is an overhead reservoir next to us, but the infrastructure required to bring water into our homes simply doesn’t exist. We are paying water tax as part of our property tax and then paying again for tankers.” Power Problems Add To Residents’ Misery If traffic and water shortages were not enough, residents say unstable electricity supply has become yet another daily struggle.“So many appliances have been damaged because of voltage fluctuations,” said Tilekar. “Almost every day, someone reports a short circuit or a damaged appliance.”Residents point out that the issue has already been acknowledged at the highest levels. In July 2023, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis reportedly raised the need for additional land allocation for an MSEDCL substation to strengthen power infrastructure in Charholi.While the proposal was subsequently approved, locals say there is little evidence of work starting on the ground. For a locality marketed as Pune’s future growth corridor, residents say the future continues to remain frustratingly out of reach.Until the promised roads, water infrastructure and power upgrades materialise, many in Charholi feel they are living in a township that is expanding rapidly but remains disconnected from the city around it.Civic Body Blames Terrain For Water Supply Woes Vijay Singh Bhosale, executive engineer of PCMC’s water supply department, said the township was facing water supply issues because it was located on elevated terrain.“The area is uphill, making it difficult to pump water to the storage tank near the township. We have already laid a pipeline and are planning to build another tank at a lower level to collect water and then pump it to the exist ing tank for distribution to the societies. However, this depends on receiving additional water from Bhama Askhed. At present, there is no alternative solution. The issue will be resolved once we are able to lift more water from Bhama Askhed,” Bhosale said.TOI also contacted the builder to understand coordination undertaken with civic authorities. Arvind Jain, managing director of Pride Group, said the company had been consistently engaging with the corporation to address residents’ concerns.“Connectivity within PCMC limits is largely adequate, but the airport link has remained stalled for years. A land acquisition issue involving a missing road link has now been resolved through efforts by our legal team and the corporation’s legal team. I have also invested funds to help move the project forward. Once the land is acquired, the road can be con structed, easing connectivity issues. Traffic congestion towards Vimannagar persists because of narrow roads, but the corporation is working on widening them. Development work on Porwal Road, Bharat Mata Road and Dhanori Road is also under way, and at least two of these stretches should see improvement by the end of the year,” Jain said.On water supply, Jain said necessary infrastructure was in place and PCMC was providing water, though the quantity might be insufficient.“There is no infra related water issue, but there are financial challenges associated with procuring tanker water. To support residents, we are providing tankers to societies at subsidised rates.We remain in constant touch with civic authorities to help resolve issues and minimise inconvenience to residents,” he addedYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: A Tennessee family wants to turn about 850 acres near the Hiwassee River into an energy campus that could host a data center; residents are raising concerns ahead of the first votes
articles.summary: US News: A proposed industrial campus in Bradley County, Tennessee, is putting economic development, energy demand and environmental protection on a collision .
articles.body: A proposed industrial campus in Bradley County, Tennessee, is putting economic development, energy demand and environmental protection on a collision course. The Wright family, owners of Wright Brothers Construction, wants to rezone and annex about 850 acres west of Interstate 75 and north of Old Lower River Road, close to the Hiwassee River. Called Project River, the development could include a power complex fuelled by natural gas and woody biomass, along with a large industrial customer such as a data center. No data center operator has signed a contract, but developers say that is the most likely use. As reported by WUTC’s Scenic Roots, the project is approaching its first planning commission and city council votes while residents continue asking questions about water, noise, traffic, emissions and the river’s future.A major proposal in a rural settingProject River would transform land that is currently zoned for farming and agricultural use. The site is privately owned by the Wright family and lies near the Hiwassee River, a waterway important to recreation, wildlife and the identity of the surrounding community.The proposed campus has been described as an $11.3 billion investment that could create about 2,600 jobs and bring advanced industrial activity to Bradley County. Developers say the project could support energy intensive manufacturing, robotics, semiconductor production or a data center. Although the public conversation has focused heavily on artificial intelligence and data processing, the final industrial customer has not yet been selected.That uncertainty is central to the debate. Residents are being asked to consider rezoning and annexation before knowing precisely what will operate on the land. Developers have said a data center is the most likely option, but there is no confirmed operator or power customer at this stage. The project’s energy infrastructure would be built first, with the eventual customer determined later.Power at the centreThe plan calls for up to 1,500 megawatts of on site electricity generation. That would include a 500 megawatt woody biomass plant and two natural gas plants with a combined capacity of 1,000 megawatts. A connection to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid would provide up to 360 megawatts for backup and periods of high demand.Developers describe the arrangement as a way to avoid shifting the project’s primary electricity demand onto local households and businesses. They say the campus would generate most of its own power and would not raise residents’ electricity bills.The proposed biomass facility would use pine trees and other woody material from the region. Supporters say that could revive local forestry operations and create new demand for timber suppliers, truckers and skilled workers. The natural gas plants would provide dependable energy when renewable or biomass generation could not meet the campus’s needs.Critics question whether a project that relies on large natural gas plants and extensive biomass burning should be presented as an environmentally responsible development. They are also seeking detailed information about fuel supply, emissions, ash disposal, truck traffic and the long term effects of operating such a large energy complex beside the river.Why residents are concernedAt public meetings, residents have raised concerns about the scale of the proposal and the limited information available before the first votes. Water, electricity, noise and environmental impacts have been recurring topics.The Hiwassee River is central to many residents’ concerns. People use the river for boating, fishing, swimming and recreation. Businesses along its shoreline depend on visitors, while nearby landowners worry that construction and industrial operations could change the character of the area.Residents have asked whether the project could affect groundwater, erosion, wildlife habitat and river water quality. They also want to know how construction would manage stormwater and sediment, particularly on a large site near a major waterway.Developers have stated that the project would not use municipal water or draw water from the Hiwassee River for daily operations. They have also said there would be no intake or discharge pipe running into the river. Those assurances have not resolved all concerns, partly because detailed environmental and traffic studies were still pending when residents began asking questions.The data centre questionData centres have become controversial across the United States because of their enormous electricity requirements, cooling systems, construction footprints and potential noise. Project River has attracted similar scrutiny even though the developers say they do not yet have a data centre contract.A data centre is the most likely customer for the proposed 1,500 megawatts, according to project leaders. The facility could support cloud computing, artificial intelligence or other high demand digital services. Such operations can bring investment and jobs, but they require reliable electricity around the clock and extensive supporting infrastructure.For residents, the uncertainty creates a trust problem. They want to know whether the community is being asked to approve a general industrial campus or a project designed primarily for a data centre. The distinction affects questions about cooling, backup generation, noise, security, water use and future expansion.Developers have said the site could also host advanced manufacturing, robotics or semiconductor production. They argue that developing the power supply first gives Bradley County flexibility to attract a range of industries rather than depending on one tenant.What supporters seeSupporters view Project River as a potential economic turning point. The proposal could bring billions of dollars in private investment, create construction and permanent jobs, increase the local tax base and support regional suppliers.The biomass plant could also create a new market for timber and forestry businesses. Supporters say the project could help maintain land based jobs and give local workers opportunities without requiring them to move away.Union representatives have expressed support for the project, pointing to the skilled construction and power plant jobs it could create. The economic argument is especially important in communities seeking higher paying employment and new industrial investment.Developers also say that the campus would be built in phases over about five years. That would spread construction activity over time and allow studies, engineering work and permitting to proceed in stages.For supporters, the project represents a chance to prepare Bradley County for industries that will require substantial electricity. They argue that data processing, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence are becoming important parts of the national economy, and rural areas should not be excluded from those opportunities.What opponents fearOpponents are not convinced that the potential benefits outweigh the risks. They worry about converting agricultural land into a large industrial complex and placing heavy infrastructure close to the Hiwassee River.Noise is another concern. A power campus and data centre could operate continuously, creating a steady industrial sound that residents say could affect homes, marinas and recreational areas. Construction traffic and ongoing deliveries may also increase pressure on local roads.Some residents question whether promised jobs will go to local workers or whether the project will rely on specialised employees recruited from elsewhere. Others want guarantees that public services, emergency response and roads will be able to support the development without placing hidden costs on taxpayers.The lack of a confirmed end user has intensified these concerns. Residents say they need complete information before local governments approve zoning and annexation changes that could be difficult to reverse.The planning processThe Wright family has applied to the City of Cleveland to rezone and annex approximately 850 acres. The site is west of Interstate 75 and north of Old Lower River Road NW. The first votes from Cleveland’s planning commission and city council are expected later in September.Before construction can begin, the project would need to pass through additional review. Environmental, ecological, geological and traffic studies are expected to play important roles. The site’s proximity to the river means stormwater management and erosion controls will be particularly important.Rezoning would change the legal framework governing the land. Annexation would bring it into the city’s jurisdiction, affecting planning, services and future development decisions. That is why residents are treating the first votes as significant even though they would not immediately authorise every stage of construction.Public meetings have become an important part of the process, but some attendees have criticised the format. At least one meeting required residents to submit questions in advance, and some said their questions were not answered directly. Developers scheduled another meeting at the PIE Center in Cleveland to continue presenting the proposal and responding to concerns.A test of transparencyProject River’s future may depend as much on public trust as on engineering. Large developments require technical studies, but communities also need clear and timely information. Residents want to know who will own and operate the power facilities, what emissions are expected, how fuel will be transported, how water will be managed and what happens if the anticipated data centre never arrives.Developers have said they are not hiding the possibility of a data centre and that the project was designed with one in mind. They also emphasise that other industrial customers remain possible. That distinction may be legally important, but it does not eliminate the need for detailed public discussion.Trust is particularly difficult when a project is announced at enormous scale before all contracts and studies are complete. Supporters see flexibility and future opportunity. Opponents see uncertainty and a risk that local officials will approve infrastructure before residents understand its full consequences.What happens nextThe immediate next step is the local review of rezoning and annexation. Residents, developers, environmental groups, unions and elected officials are expected to continue making their cases before the first formal votes.If the proposals advance, the project would move into more detailed planning and environmental review. If they are rejected or delayed, the developers may need to revise the design, identify a confirmed industrial customer or provide additional studies.Regardless of the outcome, the debate has already changed the conversation about Bradley County’s future. Project River has raised questions about how rural communities should evaluate data centres, how power intensive industries should be located and how economic development can coexist with river protection.For residents near the Hiwassee, the central issue is simple. They want to know whether the promised jobs and investment can be delivered without sacrificing the waterway, quiet and rural character that make the area home. Project River is now moving toward the votes that may determine whether that question leads to a new industrial era or a demand for a different plan.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: For 20 years, Jersey City neighbors grew tomatoes and peppers on a private lot; after building permits were issued, council voted 7-0 to advance a $1.2 million purchase to save the garden
articles.summary: US News: For two decades, a small lot on Glenwood Avenue in Jersey City served as more than an empty parcel between buildings. Neighbours turned it into a comm.
articles.body: For two decades, a small lot on Glenwood Avenue in Jersey City served as more than an empty parcel between buildings. Neighbours turned it into a community garden, growing tomatoes, peppers and other produce while creating a shared place to meet, work and learn. That informal arrangement changed when the property owner obtained permits for development, raising the possibility that the garden would disappear beneath a new building. After months of advocacy, the Jersey City City Council voted 7-0 on an initial reading to advance a $1.2 million purchase of the 128 Glenwood Avenue property for a pocket park and community garden. As reported by Daily Hudson, the proposal could preserve one of the neighbourhood’s few green gathering spaces, although the purchase still requires final approval and a clear plan for long term operation.A garden built by neighboursThe Glenwood Avenue garden developed through years of local effort rather than as a formal city park. Residents planted vegetables, maintained beds and created a shared space in a neighbourhood where open land is scarce. Tomatoes and peppers became part of the garden’s identity, but the value of the lot extended beyond what it produced.Community gardens often function as social infrastructure. People who might not otherwise meet share tools, exchange advice and help care for the land. Children learn where food comes from, older residents pass along gardening knowledge and families gain access to fresh produce. In a dense city, even a modest lot can provide a sense of space and connection.The Glenwood garden also represented continuity. For about 20 years, residents treated the property as part of their neighbourhood, even though they did not own it. That arrangement remained stable until the land changed hands and development plans moved forward.Development plans threaten the spaceThe property owner obtained building permits, creating a real possibility that the garden would be replaced by a new residential project. A developer had reportedly purchased the lot in 2022 for $425,000 and planned a small apartment building with three and four bedroom units.The competing priorities were immediately clear. Jersey City needs housing, including larger units for families, but it also needs open space and community facilities. In a neighbourhood where vacant land is limited, preserving a garden can mean giving up a potential development site.For gardeners, the issue was not simply a disagreement over property use. The lot had become a place where residents invested time, labour and emotional energy. Losing it would mean more than losing planting beds. It would remove a space that had supported local relationships for years.The threat prompted the McGinley Square Community Board and other advocates to campaign for the city to acquire the property. Their effort included collecting signatures, contacting elected officials and asking residents across Jersey City to support preserving the garden.A city purchase moves forwardAfter extended community advocacy, the City Council approved an ordinance on first reading to purchase 128 Glenwood Avenue for $1.2 million. The vote was 7-0, with Ward E Councilwoman Eleana Little and Councilwoman at-Large Mamta Singh absent.The proposed purchase would convert the site into a pocket park with a community garden. The term “pocket park” refers to a small public green space that serves a concentrated neighbourhood rather than a large regional park. Such spaces can provide seating, planting areas, shade and informal recreation within densely built communities.The vote did not complete the transaction. The purchase ordinance must receive a second and final reading. A resolution related to using Community Development Block Grant Public Facilities funding was withdrawn and expected to return at a later meeting.That means the garden’s future remains dependent on the final approval, funding arrangements and operating agreement. The first vote was an important step, but it was not yet a guarantee that the city would take ownership.How the purchase may be fundedThe proposed funding plan includes about $1 million from Community Development Block Grant money and $230,000 from the city’s liquid fund, according to reporting on the proposal.Using public funds has sparked debate. Supporters view the purchase as an investment in open space, food growing and community wellbeing. Critics question whether the city should spend $1.2 million on a garden while facing other financial pressures and housing needs. The property’s development potential adds to the disagreement because the city would be choosing to preserve land rather than permit new housing.The debate reflects a wider challenge in urban planning. Land can serve several public purposes at once, but a single parcel cannot always accommodate them all. Building homes may address housing demand, while preserving a garden may support health, community and environmental goals.The decision therefore involves more than the price of the property. It asks how city officials value different forms of public benefit and whether small green spaces deserve protection even when they sit on valuable development land.From private lot to public parkIf the purchase is completed, the site would move from private ownership into city control. The administration has discussed placing the property into Jersey City’s Adopt-A-Lot programme and issuing a request for proposals for a nonprofit operator. The likely operator would be the McGinley Square Community Board, which has led the campaign to preserve the garden.Under the proposed arrangement, the city would retain ownership while leasing the lot to a nonprofit for a nominal fee. The operator would handle maintenance, programming and fundraising. The garden would also be expected to remain open to the public for a set number of hours during the main growing season.This structure could preserve the community’s role while giving the city a framework for accountability. A nonprofit operator with strong local ties may understand the garden’s needs better than a distant contractor. At the same time, the city would need to establish clear standards for maintenance, access, safety and financial reporting.The model would also require reliable volunteer support. Community gardens often depend on a small number of highly committed people, and their workload can become unsustainable without broader participation.What the garden providesA pocket garden can offer benefits that are difficult to measure in financial terms. Vegetation helps reduce heat, absorbs rainwater and provides habitat for insects and birds. Planting beds can improve access to fresh produce and encourage healthier eating habits.The garden may also help residents cope with the pressures of city life. Gardening provides outdoor activity, opportunities for social contact and a visible connection to seasonal change. In a dense neighbourhood, the ability to step into a green space can have an impact that extends beyond the plants themselves.For children, the garden can serve as an informal classroom. A tomato plant offers a direct lesson in biology, patience and food production. A compost bin can introduce concepts of decomposition and waste reduction. These experiences may be especially valuable for young people who have limited access to private yards or rural spaces.The garden’s value is therefore not limited to the produce harvested. It is also a place for education, recreation and community identity.The question of accessSupporters want the land preserved as a community resource, but questions remain about how accessible it should be. Some community gardens divide plots among members, while others operate collectively. Some allow the public to walk through the site or attend events, while others focus on cultivation.The city’s Adopt-A-Lot framework is expected to require the garden to remain open for at least 20 hours a week from May through November. That requirement would provide public access while allowing the nonprofit operator to manage planting and maintenance.Finding the right balance will matter. Gardeners need secure space to grow food and store tools, but a pocket park should also serve residents who do not have a plot. Seating, educational programmes, produce sharing and seasonal events could help ensure that the site functions as both a garden and a public park.Clear rules established before the purchase is completed could prevent future misunderstandings.A decision about neighbourhood characterThe Glenwood Avenue dispute is part of a larger conversation about what makes a neighbourhood liveable. Housing, open space and community facilities all matter, but development pressure often forces cities to prioritise one over another.For the residents who cultivated the lot for 20 years, the garden represents a form of neighbourhood character that cannot easily be recreated after construction. Once a garden is replaced by a building, the social relationships and local knowledge built around it may be difficult to restore elsewhere.For housing advocates, the same land may represent an opportunity to provide homes in a transit connected urban area. Their concern is that preserving every informal green space can make it harder to meet housing demand and may shift development pressure to other sites.The council’s 7-0 vote does not eliminate that tension. It signals that a majority of participating council members believe preserving this particular lot is worth advancing, but the broader debate about land use will continue.What happens nextThe next steps include a second and final council reading on the purchase ordinance, further consideration of the funding resolution and negotiations over the property’s future operation. If approved, the city will need to complete the acquisition, prepare the land and establish the nonprofit management arrangement.The transition may take time. The lot will require planning, soil assessment, infrastructure improvements and possibly new garden beds or fencing. A successful pocket park will depend on more than the purchase itself. It will need a sustainable budget, committed volunteers and a clear programme of public activities.For now, the council vote has given the Glenwood garden a chance to survive. The tomatoes and peppers that once grew on a private lot may continue to grow under a new public arrangement, surrounded by the same neighbours who spent years tending them.The proposed purchase is ultimately a decision about whether a small piece of land can carry large civic value. In Jersey City, residents are arguing that it can.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
